embedded.caption: Thomas et al. (2017), Supplemental video 2. Histioteuthis heteropsis makes ratcheting turns.
embedded.teaching_note: Cockeyed squids make repeated changes in orientation described as ratcheting turns. The original recordings document living animals changing body direction while retaining the characteristic arrangement of their unequal eyes relative to the surrounding water column. A turn changes locomotor orientation and the visual scene at the same time. Maintaining useful viewing directions requires coordination between body posture and the positions of the sensory organs, linking a movement pattern to the acquisition of visual information. The study compared posture across two histioteuthid species. Their shared eye asymmetry and upward-versus-downward viewing pattern connect a recurring behavioral arrangement to the visual demands imposed by directionally unequal light in the deep ocean.

embedded.caption: Thomas et al. (2017), Supplementary video 1. Close-up of unequal squid eyes.
embedded.teaching_note: A lens filter selectively absorbs part of the light passing toward a retina. Thomas and colleagues recorded yellow pigmentation in the large eye of some cockeyed squids and examined transmission through lenses recovered from captured animals. Pigmentation changes the spectrum reaching the photoreceptors. The large eye's filtering is associated with the upward-looking visual task, in which the animal encounters residual sunlight and possible bioluminescent signals superimposed on that background. Filtering can change the relationship between signal and background before receptor activation occurs. The eye's optical structures therefore participate in sensory selection alongside the retina, providing an anatomical mechanism for modifying the visual information delivered to neural tissue.

embedded.conversion: Compatibility H.264/yuv420p and AAC where present; original resolution, scene, normal timing and audio preserved, CRF18.
embedded.caption: Thomas et al. (2017), Supplemental video 3. Stigmatoteuthis dofleini changes orientation.
embedded.teaching_note: Thomas and colleagues used optical modeling to compare detection of silhouettes with detection of bioluminescent point sources. A point source is a luminous object small enough to occupy a restricted angular region in the visual scene. Increasing eye size improves photon collection, but the benefit depends on the visual task. Their analysis supported a greater benefit of a large upward-looking eye for detecting silhouettes against the dim background than for the downward-looking point-source task. This task dependence explains why the two eyes need not be equally large. Investing in one enlarged eye can improve the task most sensitive to photon collection while retaining a smaller eye for luminous targets in the darker direction.

embedded.caption: Burford & Robison (2020), Movie S1. Humboldt squid pigmentation during in situ activity.
embedded.teaching_note: A foraging squid changes arm and body position while producing pigmentation patterns. Burford and Robison connected particular visual components to the sequence surrounding feeding, using in situ recordings that preserved the animal's natural behavioral context. Prey capture combines orientation, approach, and coordinated use of the arms. Changes in pigmentation occur within that motor sequence, allowing a nearby animal to receive visual information about the activity of the foraging squid. The original supplementary movie supplies the recorded movement and pattern transitions. The paper's coded observations connect those transitions to behavioral context, separating the chronology of a feeding event from a static description of the skin pattern.

embedded.caption: Stuckless et al. (2023), Video S2. Blocking and shared feeding by Ceramaster granularis.
embedded.teaching_note: Ceramaster granularis can change its route or position when another sea star occupies the path or food. Stuckless and colleagues recorded blocking, wedging, and shared access during experiments involving animals of different relative sizes. Wedging is movement under another animal to gain access to the food beneath it. This tactic connects arm and body contact to a change in feeding position, rather than requiring displacement of the entire competitor. The supplementary recording preserves interactions among individuals around the same food source. Their positions and movements connect encounter with a conspecific to access decisions, explaining why body size alone does not determine the outcome of competition in this preparation. This is an author-provided time-lapse record. Recorded speed is preserved, and behavioral durations come from the article rather than the movie playback duration.

embedded.caption: Stuckless et al. (2023), Video S4. Hippasteria phrygiana skirts a neighbor.
embedded.teaching_note: Hippasteria phrygiana often approached food along a straight path until another individual occupied the route. Stuckless and colleagues recorded animals moving around neighbors rather than consistently climbing across their bodies. Skirting changes the path while preserving approach toward the resource. Brief contact between arm tips accompanies this interaction, linking local information from another animal to adjustment of locomotor direction. The behavior contrasts with wedging in Ceramaster granularis. Coexisting deep-sea sea stars use different contact-related tactics around a shared resource, so a common food stimulus can produce species-specific movement sequences rather than a single universal competitive response. This is an author-provided time-lapse record. Recorded speed is preserved, and behavioral durations come from the article rather than the movie playback duration.

embedded.caption: Stuckless et al. (2023), Video S7. Henricia lisa taps food with an arm tip.
embedded.teaching_note: Henricia lisa displayed repeated arm-tip contact with food. Stuckless and colleagues described the tip being applied to and lifted from the food with limited displacement, distinguishing this activity from continuous locomotion toward the source. This tapping behavior included successive contacts separated by roughly three minutes and movements of about one centimeter. The temporal pattern provides a repeatable way to characterize how the animal interacts with food after reaching it. Contact behavior links acquisition of local information to handling rather than to distant approach. The distinction separates orientation toward a resource from the actions used to inspect or consume it, both of which contribute to successful feeding in darkness. This is an author-provided time-lapse record. Recorded speed is preserved, and behavioral durations come from the article rather than the movie playback duration.

embedded.caption: Stuckless et al. (2023), Video S8. Buccinum scalariforme approaches food.
embedded.teaching_note: The gastropod Buccinum scalariforme approached food in the same experimental environment as the sea stars. Its movement uses a muscular foot rather than radial arms, providing a different anatomical route from sensory information to locomotion. Stuckless and colleagues documented food-directed trajectories and interactions with other animals at the resource. The approach recording preserves the movement of the intact animal, complementing the trajectory and feeding measurements reported in the paper. Comparing gastropod and sea-star behavior separates shared ecological demands from different motor organization. Both can locate and approach food under dark conditions, but their body structures constrain how they move around a neighbor and establish access to the resource. This is an author-provided time-lapse record. Recorded speed is preserved, and behavioral durations come from the article rather than the movie playback duration.

embedded.caption: Golikov et al. (2023), Supplementary Video 01 (excerpt). Cirroteuthis muelleri spreads its web near the bottom at 3693 m.
embedded.teaching_note: Bottom-associated Cirroteuthis muelleri performed a recurring sequence involving arm-web spreading, enveloping, and retreat. The web is the tissue connecting the arms, expanding the surface that can enclose a region beneath the animal. Golikov and colleagues recorded sequences lasting 11–21 seconds. The ordered phases connect movement of a large anatomical structure to the location of potential prey on the bottom, giving the behavior a repeatable spatial and temporal organization. The original video observations preserve the transition between open and enveloping postures. These transitions support the feeding interpretation because they repeatedly place the arm-web system around bottom material before the animal withdraws from the enclosed patch. This is a temporal excerpt from the original article-linked ROV recording. Source timestamps and conversion details are recorded in media_sources.json; original resolution and playback speed are preserved.

embedded.caption: Golikov et al. (2023), Supplementary Video 03 (excerpt). Cirroteuthis muelleri contacts the bottom and retreats at 1506 m.
embedded.teaching_note: During the enveloping phase, the cirrate octopod brings its arm-web system around a section of the seafloor. Golikov and colleagues interpreted this phase as prey capture and recorded variable durations associated with the capture activity. Reported capture phases lasted 5–49 seconds. The difference between the recurring overall movement sequence and the time spent enclosing a patch connects stereotyped motor organization to variation in local feeding circumstances. Retreat returns the animal from the enclosed position to movement away from the patch. The sequence therefore couples encounter, enclosure, and withdrawal, contrasting with the filament-based collection of vampire squid and the pursuit-associated feeding of Humboldt squid. This is a temporal excerpt from the original article-linked ROV recording. Source timestamps and conversion details are recorded in media_sources.json; original resolution and playback speed are preserved.
